parsed_answer.content:
When designing modern Java applications involving temporal logic, developers frequently stumble over the distinction between Period and Duration. Introduced in Java 8 as part of the `java.time` package (JSR-310), these two classes address fundamentally different representations of time-based amounts. While both measure the elapsed time between two points, they operate on completely separate temporal scales and follow distinct arithmetic models.

A Period models an amount of time in terms of calendar-based units—specifically years, months, and days. It is inherently tied to human-centric calendar systems and handles variable-length time segments like leap years, daylight saving time shifts, and varying month lengths (e.g., February versus March). Conversely, a Duration measures time in exact, machine-readable units—specifically seconds and nanoseconds. It represents an absolute physical length of time devoid of calendar anomalies, making it ideal for high-precision performance logging, thread timeouts, and asynchronous execution tracking. Confusing these two often leads to subtle bugs, such as calculating financial interest using strict nano-second durations instead of calendar-bound periods, or vice versa.

rows: Adjusts based on calendar rules and local dates
Absolute elapsed time (e.g., strictly 86,400 seconds per day)

items: Period calculations are heavily dependent on the underlying Chronology. Adding a Period of 1 month to January 31st yields February 28th (or 29th) due to calendar clamping rules.
Duration instances are immutable and thread-safe. They store time as a combination of seconds (long) and nanoseconds (int), making them optimal for low-latency calculations.

Attempting to obtain a Duration between two LocalDate instances will throw an UnsupportedTemporalTypeException because LocalDate lacks time-of-day precision required for nanosecond accuracy; you must use ChronoUnit.DAYS or Period instead.

parsed_answer.content: A common production trap occurs when developers use Duration to compute time spans across daylight saving time boundaries for scheduling tasks. Because a Duration measures fixed 24-hour days as 86,400 seconds, scheduling an event 'Duration.ofDays(1)' ahead across a DST transition will trigger the job an hour early or late relative to local wall-clock time. Always use Period for calendar-aligned operations and Duration strictly for physical machine-time measurements.

title: What is the difference between Period and Duration?
